Eva Berry would have walked ten miles to get to the fair that year. When she was a kid the county owned the fairgrounds, just as it owned the courthouse lawn, the sewage treatment plant, the landfill. The fair was a place for everyone, and nobody called it "the fairgrounds." You called it "the fair," just as you called your hometown "town," or "the town," without the "smith" or "chester" or the "ville."

Of course the county couldn't afford everything anymore, so different organizations had to share this fair or that fair. Once the 4-H lost the livestock auction, the fire department shuttled people a half-hour drive to their kids' competitions, and then the 4-H got no applicants for their fair board. Now the fair was put on by an organization based in Kentucky, with exhibits and horse events Eva didn't understand at all. Besides, she was thirty-one years old, and the 4-H board still called her "dear." Eva had heard women used to put the 4-H before their families. She couldn't imagine doing that.

Still, she had asked off Saturday from the Family Dollar so she could spend the day at home playing softball at the fair, or taking her kids to the wheelbarrow races-or whatever the county would put on. And there was a barbecue they always had. She didn't think they'd be able to afford it, but at the last minute, when Ernest took his paycheck to the bank, he deposited Alan's on accident. The guy had given him two tickets. Say good-bye to Saturday-night sleeping-in and the cheap date movie.

Now all that was left was the meat draw, for the contest in which Eva made their grand entry prize every year. She let her finger nail flick back one more chicken wing. It was still warm, moist, freshly coated with white pepper, paprika, salt, and garlic. She knew she would lick her finger if she weren't in public, and maybe if she were alone she would finish the whole wing. She had caught Alan finishing things in the refrigerator, like the half-and-half, or virgins like Alan's little sister, Jenny. But she knew the way he looked at her at mass. The river, he knew, was filling like he'd never seen it over the mouth of Millers Creek, less than a mile upstream. The negligence that could be charged to his actions was small in this world, but he'd never forgiven himself for the one time he'd needed something from a river and it wasn't there, taking with it a man Dale had known for twenty years. Now his wife had made a mockery of Dale's plans, and Dale had to hold back tears or lose his voice despite himself.

"Shit, Dale, I don't know either," Hank said.

Dale killed the call, drove his truck home, rang Ann for twenty minutes while it was still light and they both had the breath for it. When the call ended, Dale looked out the window. He'd been breathing bees from the edge of a skirt around a pollinated meadow, and in that memory he and Ann remembered each other, twenty-five years ago, a hot apartment, the same aluminum wind-rattle on the fire escape, phones ringing and closing from down the hall, shut windows practically bursting in their frames, and the air not quite stale enough to need opening. He told Ann he could make this beach for her, by the ocean, anytime it was perfect, then closed his eyes and let the phone drop to his chest. Ann's voicemail had been a restless background, like the bees, and Dale lay down on it.

When he woke, his head felt muddled, and his hand was dead of pins. He rubbed it to life again, reached for his phone, unlocked it, and tripped.

When he woke, she was already calling the ambulance.

Dale showed up to work Saturday morning and ordered barricades and warning flags just in case, then drove to the fairgrounds. He saw a yard full of U-Haul trucks and a hundred teenage girls in shorts getting out. He wore his black dress shoes and a new suit, and he watched as the state's Congressman hosted a breakfast in the barn while people kept walking across the bridge.

Dale bet with himself. Three hours, he thought. The bridge wasn't going to make it three hours. But when the bridge passed traffic stop in hand, he grinned at himself and ordered his crews home. He sat and watched the people coming in: bright sunlight on new bikini tops, fritter oil glistening on bags of sticks of beef and pork, the breeze through the trees. Then something caught his eye. It was a jagged piece of metal sticking out of the asphalt. Dale wiped the sweat off his brow. It reminded him of the Harry and Elsie Kay bridge back in '09, where the plates on the leading edge of the beams were starting to rock off.

Dale handed his wife the phone while he watched the machine-plant show, and Ann smiled as Hank thanked her for making her "everyman" jelly cakes. He said that next year the county would have new giant inflatables, and, after Hank spoke, Dale heard Ann whisper "Goody Two-Shoes."

Hank went on: "This is an awful lot of wedding planning, Margaret," he said, then he must have heard her coming. "One sec," he told Ann—and then Dale heard "No, wait!" far away.

Ann hung up and took his hand. "Maggie's folks called to let them talk," she said. She was smiling. Dale smiled too. He was starting to get what Hank meant that morning.

The Miller's Creek bridge fell down nine months after Dale shut it off, on a flood day. He was on the phone the whole time, in the sheriff's office, telling the divers where to find the victims' cars. In pictures it took on a geometry: a man and a woman lost together in a cove downstream. The bridge simply broke.

So, ten years off Dale's pension, seven bodies, fourteen caskets, one underaged victim. And days later, the union went on strike anyway, all because of one man's job.

At eight PM, Dale Brandt got in his car and knocked the photos off his dashboard and drove home.

So. The bridge fell down.

Next morning in Chicago, I called Dale and left a message. His phone rang off the hook that day. Hank Voss and a few others blamed the bridge failure on Dale; they said he should have shut down the bridge earlier, and they let it be known that it would probably be his last act before his pension.

Eventually the inquiry swung towards the engineering firm. In the November election, Hank Voss was run out of office.

But the engineers weren't at fault. In mathspeak, they were right on the money. Closure risk is unavoidable. Bridges always fail in the moment best designed to withstand them. Insurance companies know this, and they bank on it. A bridge turnspike collects money by charging everyone who uses it, but since the day the bridge tolls started, the money has gone straight into a lockbox, and it has never, ever, been used to fund bridge repairs.

So my grandfather's traffic report was not primarily a warning about weak bridges. It was a warning about people.

In most circumstances, this is not a problem. After all, if a traffic engineer warned you that a building was one in a hundred chance of falling over tomorrow, you wouldn't begin boarding it up the next day. You know bridges do fall, but mostly they don't. In real life, the 99% are more important than the 1%.

But there are a few cases in which this is not true. The most important is terrorism. If variable x is an improbable expensive accident, terrorism is an improbable expensive willful act. You can reason with accident. Terrorism acts rationally.

In the chaos, I caught the name of a driver in the image. In front of the tractor was Eli Logan, Dale's former coworker. Enforcement of the bridge sensor began three days before, which meant that Eli was struck by falling rubble while he was driving the sensor past the bridge.

I needed to know why he was there, so I looked him up. His name showed up on an internet forum about Harlan County history. There was a post from him dated three days before the accident:

West of Miller's Creek bridge/what is wrong w/indicators

So I noticed these stones on the side of rt 394 as you go west of Miller's Creek.

In her thirty-six years, she'd had four kids, worked three jobs, and never failed to pay off a debt on time. But she couldn't afford to fix the car, any more than she could afford a toothbrush. When Dale walked in, he found Beth in the washroom, on her back, hugging her knees to her chest, her face pale, her teeth brown and broken. From fifteen feet away, the smell hit him like a drive-by slinging meth. He stepped from one puddle of urine into another. A toilet filled half the room, but there was no water in it. Most advice of the "how to sell stars" variety tells you a simple little lie: you need to sell "fake" stars, so your customers don't get the wrong idea when they do some research on how it's done. In Harlan County, population fifty-eight thousand, the twelve-man road department was certified as highway construction employees. Hank was quiet. He always listened for a while before he spoke. "You don't spend my whole career in politics without learning that if you say no often enough, sooner or later everybody starts saying yes. It's just a county fair. Are you sure your diver knows what he's talking about?"

Dale glanced at the photographs again. "I try to get competent people."

"And now you're not sure he is?"

"I didn't say that," Dale said. "All I said was that I can't be sure it's safe. I don't know how you want me to feel, Hank. I don't want anyone to get hurt."

"Think about what you're saying. If it's closed, they'll close the gates on the 4-H families who are due to compete, on the premiums those kids would win, on the money those people spent on their passes and campgrounds. They'll be furious. You ever try to head off four thousand angry moms with their kids in tow?"

"You're not going to close that bridge," Dale said.

Hank Voss sighed. "No, we're not. You make sure you've got uniformed deputies standing by the detour to direct people."

Dale waited for Hank to say good night. When he finally did, Dale took out the photos and tossed them into the catfish hole beside the road.

Darkness had fallen, and it was Saturday. Dale sat at home with the TV on and an open can of beer on the table. It was concluding a special report on the millisecond trade. Traders used to buy and sell stocks in fractions of a second - hundreds of times a day. Dale had never understood how that was different from the market forever, until tonight, when the anchor said, "The data from tonight's opening indicated that the NYSE traded 163,158 messages in the first millisecond after the open, representing a total of 600 stock transactions."

Dale had never heard anyone use the word "transaction" except with his wife's illness. A "transaction" meant something important enough to remember. This meant nothing.

"Unbelievable," the anchor said. There was an interview with a professor who said that the market had sped up because there was so much money waiting to be made. "There's no more money being made," he said. "It's a case of too many traders and not enough transactions. It's like popcorn - if you had a popcorn popper as big as Iowa, the popcorn would use up all the oil and fuel but the number of kernels would stay the same."

Dale thought about the report on the bridge. "Failure under heavy and sustained loading," it had said. The engineers had never said what was happening to the bridge - in fact, they'd never looked at it, not really. They'd used a few assumptions and a computer model. They were no smarter than the day traders, assuming that if you did things fast enough the result would take care of itself. His father had spent a lifetime on bridges. His grandfather had died building one. It had never occurred to any Brandt that a bridge could fail. Now one had, and nobody asked how. The load was too much, and the bridge was too weak. Why go into it?

Someone knocked on the door. It was Bobby Lake, the junior road supervisor. He said he'd come to help with the traffic.

"Jesus, Dale - you're not really closing it, are you?"

Dale shook his head. "The piers are undermined. I got the engineer back on the phone and he said - look. We don't know what's going to happen with that bridge.

Dale picked up the diver, Owen Munson, early Friday. Owen lived in Hays, the county seat, and Dale drove while Owen told him about the April flood.

"There was more water than I ever saw," Owen said as they turned west on Route 105. Maybe God just didn't want the county to lose me."

Dale smiled. Owen always talked too much. He woke up the next morning at five. He lay in bed a long while and heard the birds and thought of the way Hank had said "or not." It sounded so final, like a verdict. Why was he spending a Friday at work--and $70 in gas--when he'd decided already? A slow anger crawled through him. It was his bridge, not Hank's. Why was he letting Hank tell him what to do? He got up and shaved, got into his county pickup, and drove toward the bridge.

In his rearview mirror, past the far trees and the filling station, he saw a cloud of dust rising from the county road. As he neared the bridge, the dust braided into tails of exhaust, a zipper of heavy tires climbing the embankment and through the girders of the west abutment. A string of twenty-high cattle trailers shuddered into the parking lot like the cars of an international caravan. By the time he stopped beneath the bridge, every lot was full. The only space left was the handicapped spot, right beneath the bridge.

He cut off the ignition and sat for a long moment, letting the silence settle over him like a cloak. The dust took its time settling too, and he listened to the birdsong again, feeling it wrap through him now like a bright chord. He took a deep, grateful breath. The trailers had no permits, and they'd caused a safety hazard by backing up to the bridge abutments. He would tell the drivers so, although it was too late to turn them around.

As he stepped out of the truck, the wind shifted, and a dry, earthy smell rolled up from the water. The creek's banks were caked in rust-red mud, and the water ran brown and sluggish. He took the ninety steps down to the dive shop on his knees. When Dale got home his wife met him on the porch. "You were wrong, weren't you," she said. He looked at her, and then he went inside and opened the cabinet over the sink, took out the pills. They were half the size of aspirins, round, milky-white. Ann took two in the morning and two at night.

"I was wrong," he said, and he poured the pills into the sink. They fizzed and dissolved, and he flushed the water. When he turned, Ann was standing in the doorway, her arms folded.

"What are we going to do now?" she said.

Dale didn't answer. He waited until she turned and went back inside. He finished up his beer, then went into the bedroom and got the first aid kit from the bottom drawer of the dresser. He lifted his shirt and smeared antibacterial ointment across the red gash along his right side. It came up to his ribs, and his hip, and it hurt, but he didn't mind. It wasn't the worst he'd done.

Every spring he went out there and looked at the bridge, then he called Harlan County, talked to the supervising engineer, reviewed the report. Nineteen years, and every time the answer was the same. Then, Ann, dying. That was new.

He turned off the light and went out onto the porch. Down by the creek the water was low and fast. Through the window he could see the house, sitting on the ridge above the wind in the pines. He loved it here. Always had.

He went back inside and rinsed the ointment off his hands, tossed the tube in the trash and closed the lid. He put on his boots and took the keys off the hook. He took a flashlight and the little yellow gut kit from the back of the closet. He turned off the porch light, locked the door behind him and got into the truck. He turned down the road toward the bridge. It was Friday night, and far away over the ridges he could hear the sop and whistle of the frogs.

Dale stood and looked across the bridge. He couldn't feel the ground tremble with the weight of all the stuff he carried. He only knew it was there, weighing him down. Bridge men drowned themselves. He had the names in his head and the stories, where they'd jumped and how they'd been found.

He thought about the two boys in the pickup, upstream. His hands came off the wheel and went away, like they'd move on their own. When they came back, he was standing on the other side of the bridge.

We've just crossed the Rubicon," Hank said. He was drinking a highball with a microbewheat name Dale couldn't pronounce. "God help us if we're wrong."

The Beginning

In the beginning, before there were proper roads, there were footpaths. Loops and arcs, likeFermat's Theorem claims, connecting the points that mattered: village to village, shearing shed to creek, homestead to field. When roads became essential in the American backcountry, settlers blazed them, often clearing no more than a double-width track through brush and undergrowth. Where the feet of men and horses, wheels and oxen, already compressed the earth, pioneers left them, and rocks and fallen logs marked their courses for decades. These routes and traces moved with the towns they served, meandering back and forth across the contour map like a student's doodles, erasing even older tracks that had grown up into the forest, underneath them, before being rediscovered by the car.

When people settled in the county, they built their lives alongside these ancient routes, and the county built its first roads upon them. The survey had followed a straight line from the state road running east-west to the county schoolhouse a mile south, but soon the county work-crew veered the route back to the well-trod paths, following old lines where the trees grew tall and strait as cathedral. A hundred years passed before anybody built another road into the county.

Bridge men drowned themselves. The name stood alone on the list of occupations open to a man without a college education. It sat above "logger" but below "miner." It took a peculiar combination of fearlessness and defeat, ignorance and confidence, to drive heavy equipment off a bridge on purpose, every day. Bridge men looked away from the drop in front of them when they backed their seventeen-ton loaders off the road

"Lightning might also strike the fairgrounds during the fair," Hank interrupted. "I don't like to build barriers against every possibility, Dale. I prefer action. We will open the bridge and you will monitor it. You understand?"

"Monitor it? I'm not a bridge inspector."

"I'm sure there's someone you can hire," Hank said. "It seems you brought in a structural engineer already. Get him back out there and tell him to pronounce it safe and you'll be fine with the county."

"Engineers don't work that way. It's not ethical."

Hank sighed. "It's not ethical to cancel a hundred-year-old tradition over uncertainty, either. Remember that, Dale." He hung up, and Dale, his hands trembling a little although the night was mild, cleared the photos off his hood and drove home.

On Friday morning Dale called the engineering firm and narrated Hank's order. "I'll tell you what, Dale," the engineer said. "If the county wants to accept the risk, we can be out there Monday morning bright and early, and if the piers are all right, we'll call it so. But if they're not, and they want to put the county on notice, we'll make it official then."

"That's fine," Dale said, but he knew it wasn't. He was not going to risk driving across the bridge himself, let alone a bus full of kids. He called the county sheriff and the state police, laid out the situation for them, and asked them what they would do if he closed the road. They both said they'd handle traffic somehow, but the county would pay for it. He asked if they'd accept responsibility if a car went into the creek. They said they understood, but no.

There were six feet of water in Miller's Creek after the flood. More might fall with the next storm. He pictured the fairgrounds on his right, bright and lively for a day and a half, then choked off, cattle trucked away, kids disappointed, and in the middle of it all the bridge, solid maybe, maybe fatally damaged.

EVERY YEAR when he taught "The Literary Life of Theodore Dreiser" in first-year writing, Victor Losey would have at least one student approach him before the term was over to inform him that they had never read the novel he'd been lecturing on all semester. He knew they were telling the truth; the students were . There were almost forty of them in a section, every one of them eighteen or nineteen, and the pace of his lectures had left them almost no time to read beyond the weekly assignments. His classes had shrunk over the years as Merton College turned more and more to part-time, often international students of indeterminate age and motivation, but the chaotic, seat-of-the-pants vibe of the old days was pretty much gone.

In the beginning, Victor had tried to instill a little discipline, mostly by lecturing with ferocious concentration for the full hour and assigning a page or two of writing every class. He quickly realized, though, that most of the class had little if any experience as readers, let alone writers, and so he simplified his lectures and cut back the short writing assignments, which he would then spend most of his free time laboriously grading. When he returned the graded work, he found that virtually none of his margin comments had been read, which suggested to him that he might be wasting his time. But he found it almost impossible to stop. In teachers' meetings the pedagogical counsel of his colleague Mort Solomon, who taught the same course in another section, was to simplify even further and to give a single large paper at the term's end. Victor had tried this, but he ended up spending almost every night in the week before grades were due reading his students' papers while his wife paddled furiously in the pool next door. The experience made him feel old and sad.

So here he was, on the Thursday before the due date for his students' final papers, fourteen years into his career at Merton and three days past his fifty-sixth birthday. He walked across the back campus from his office to the coffee cart that had taken up residence outside Religious Studies for the summer. It was run by a bearded man in a tie-dyed T-shirt who called himself Yogi Bhuji and gave away yoga stickers with every purchase. Victor had a decaf, with a Cinnamon Dolce.

When the news hit the paper Friday, the phones at the courthouse started ringing. This time it was the county executive calling Hank, telling him to make Dale retract. He was powerless to fire Dale, but he could tarnish him. Dale would be branded stupid at best, or if the bridge stayed up, the county would spend twice as much repairing it later, and his misjudgment would cost taxpayers money. Or if it fell, Hank could find a way to hold Dale liable. Damned if you do, damned if you don't.

For now, the executive said, he would back Hank "one hundred percent." Hank could tell Dale that he was "strongly encouraged" to reverse his decision.

The call came while Dale was at supper. He put down his fork and looked at Ann. She was tired from the heat, and the medical equipment at her side hummed, making the little kitchen feel hushed and small. When Hank called, Dale told him to go to hell and hung up.

Later he sent Hank a one-word e-mail: "No."

He couldn't save twenty thousand dollars in lost tourism, or the disappointments of children who looked forward to the fair all year. He couldn't make Ann's medicine cheaper, or keep the executive from trying to bully him. The Miller's Creek bridge ran north and south with a sharp curve to the east in the center. The main span was steel girders laid on reinforced concrete decks supported by two piers on concrete piles. One pier was in the middle of the bridge where the river flowed around it; the other was at the river's edge to the west. The center pier took most of the traffic weight, and the edge could collapse without a problem. The problem was that when the water rose in a flood it roughed up the riverbed; when it receded, it left behind a cavity, or scour. Around the center pier, the scour was so deep the pile caps were exposed. That was a disaster during an earthquake, when the pier-and-foundation complex had to balance the forces acting on it. With parts of the pile caps missing, the shear stresses in the complex were almost certainly higher than they'd been designed for. The other problem the last flood had left behind was a long, deep scour trough downstream of the bridge. If anything fell off, it would hurtle through there in a powerful water jet. The engineers had worried all that through and decided not to leave it to chance: the Miller's Creek bridge was to close until it was repaired. The river was high in Dale's memory. He had heard about the old bridge from his dad: three spans, wooden timbers, concrete piles. Washed away in the big flood, Dale. Then they built the Miller's Creek bridge. Dale crossed it three times a day before being hired on to the county. In those days he was baling hay and working at the mines; he never allowed himself to notice it. If you got attached to things, you were crazy. The only thing you could count on was their going away. In 1962 his parents died within a week. Dale was nineteen. His mother had tripped off a step while cleaning their rental house, broken her knee, and died three days later in surgery. His father, a roughneck on oil wells, was in Montana. He flew home, but before the doctors at the hospital in Casper would let him see his wife she wasn't his to see, and all he got was an airplane picture of the wake with a single wreath by the graveside.

Ann had lived most of her childhood in the Smokemont community of the Great Smoky Mountains. Her dad raised and rode Tennessee Walking Horses, and Ann went with him to judge them. The Miller's Creek Bridge was built in 1948. It was 381 feet long, spanning a river half a mile wide. The east and west ends were on high ground, but the bridge's center section had to be supported in the river with two piers sunk to bedrock.

When it was dedicated, the governor called it the biggest county bridge east of the Rockies. Back when Raleigh, the county seat, was logged out, the bridge had been an economic godsend. During the Depression, the WPA built it in one of Harlan's poorest sections. The bridge opened just weeks before President Roosevelt came to town and declared Harlan the poorest county in America.

Dale's grandfather had worked on the structure. He was sent to Harlan on the assumption that it was the only place he wouldn't be lynched. One Saturday in August, after the job was done, Dale's grandfather took his money to the local bar and bought the men a drink. When he came home, his wife wasn't talking to him. They stared at each other until he realized he was still wearing his Harlan County engineering shirt. Then she gave him two weeks to move out and never look back.

Dale saw the bridge fall Saturday, sixty feet downstream of his truck. The sound was continuous, a shuddering, and he had just enough time to dive through the passenger side door onto the pavement and turn to watch it happen. The long, forty-foot steel turns flipped up and over the span, collapsing in onto itself like a deck of cards. Debris went up into the sky in a purple cloud, something like the dust of death.

Dale could see about ten cars in the air, twisting end over end. He counted five pickups or jeeps he knew. He saw a broken, bent twelve-foot section parting the rocks and trees down below. He saw a trailer full of cattle go over in a cloud of shrieking. He did not know how many people were killed.

For weeks afterward he would wake up in the middle of the night sweating, shaking, and unable to move his body. He would look up at Ann in bed, and wonder whether he should ever have answered Hank, or answered any other way, or confounded Hank with silence. Before the bridge fell, he had given his wife's health up to science, his retirement to a pension plan, and his integrity to his employer. After the bridge fell, one by one he would give all of those away, but he would not forget them. He would find a way to make America a little stronger.

Ann was dead, Hank was in jail, and Dale was three and a half years into a new job down the street at the Harlan County K-rail plant. He had started as an electrical engineer designing base components for the bridge rails, and now he was project manager for a consortium developing composite panels and deployment systems for flatbed trucks.

Dale had put in a week of twelve-hour days in a Harlan County heat wave.
